newsitem.title: USA: U.S. airlines won't predict Boeing merger impact.
newsitem.headline: U.S. airlines won't predict Boeing merger impact.

text.p: Major U.S. airlines said on Sunday it was too early to forecast the impact of a proposed $13.3 billion merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp on aircraft prices or their airplane-buying strategy.
"It is too early to tell," Delta Air Lines Inc spokesman Todd Clay said. "It is like looking into a crystal ball to tell what would be coming down the pipeline."

Earlier on Sunday, Seattle, Wash.-based Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, based in St. Louis, Mo., announced plans to merge via a stock swap, creating what they said would be the largest integrated aerospace company in the world.
But most major U.S. airlines took a wait-and-see attitude.
"We'll have to see what transpires," Northwest Airlines Corp spokesman Jon Austin said. "It's a long way from announcing a deal to consummating it."
Boeing and McDonnell Douglas said in a joint statement they expected to deal to close by mid-1997 but it was subject to approval by shareholders of both companies and certain regulatory agencies.

Boeing Chief Executive Officer Phil Condit, who said he would serve as chairman and CEO of the combined company, told a news conference: "Our best guess, and I underline the word 'guess' because there are a lot of other agenices that have to be involved, (is) that the process will be at least a six-month kind of process.
"So mid-year is our target area. It could be a little shorter," he said.
But he said he did not expect anti-trust concerns would not be a "big issue," because most of the companies' programs were complementary.
Condit told reporters he expected to file the necessary merger-related papers with the U.S. government within the next two weeks.

Continental Airlines Inc, AMR Corp and USAir Group Inc declined comment on the merger proposal, while UAL Corp, Chicago-based parent company of United Airlines, was not immediately available for comment.
Trans World Airlines Inc spokesman Mark Abels said TWA was a customer of both aircraft manufacturers, but it was not in a position to comment on competition in that industry.
"Both of these manufacturers make good aircraft, and we have aircraft on order from both," he said.

Trans World Airlines had 20 firm orders and 20 optional orders placed with Boeing for its 757 carrier, he said. "These are not all purchase orders -- some of them are leased, but they are all new aircraft," Abels said.
Abels said TWA also had 15 MD-80 Series aircraft on order from McDonnell Douglas.
Of its 191 aircraft, 111 planes were made by McDonnell Douglas and about 70 were made by Boeing, he said. The rest were made by Lockheed Martin Corp.
Southwest Airlines Co, which said its entire fleet was comprised of 243 Boeing 737 jets, said it continued to be a strong supporter of Boeing aircraft.
"In October 1997, we will be the launch customer for Boeing's 737-700 aircraft," Southwest spokesman Ginger Hardage said.
